INAH fieldwork in the Sierra de Texcoco records the dead arriving from 28 October, so Halloween night falls inside their visit.
Mexico City's Day of the Dead parade began in 2016, a year after Spectre filmed a fictional one; spectators rose from 425,000 to over 2 million by 2019.

faqs.question: Do people in Mexico celebrate Halloween?
faqs.answer: Yes. Children dress up and ask for their calaverita on 31 October, and costume nights at discos date back to the 1980s, according to one UAM scholar. For most families, though, the bigger dates are 1 and 2 November, Día de Muertos.

faqs.question: Why does Day of the Dead start right after Halloween in Mexico?
faqs.answer: Because Día de Muertos is kept on the Catholic feasts of All Saints (1 November) and All Souls (2 November), and Halloween falls on the night before All Saints. In some Nahua villages near Texcoco the dead are welcomed from 28 October, so Halloween night falls inside the visit.

faqs.question: What do Mexican kids say when they go trick-or-treating?
faqs.answer: They ask for their calaverita, the 'little skull', meaning a sweet or a coin, usually with a short sung or spoken request. Around 1970 in Mexico City, one writer recalls, children mostly received coins, not sweets.

faqs.question: Is 2 November a public holiday in Mexico?
faqs.answer: No. Article 74 of the Federal Labour Law lists the mandatory rest days, and neither 1 nor 2 November is among them. In 2026, 2 November is a Monday, and the next federal holiday is Revolution Day on Monday 16 November.

faqs.question: Which day is for children and which for adults on Day of the Dead?
faqs.answer: The common shorthand is children on 1 November and adults on 2 November, but it varies by town. In Santa Catarina del Monte, fieldwork recorded baptised children arriving on 30 October and adults on 31 October and 1 November.

faqs.question: When did the Mexico City Day of the Dead parade start?
faqs.answer: The first real parade was held in 2016, a year after the James Bond film Spectre showed a fictional one. About 1,000 performers took part, and spectator numbers grew from 425,000 in 2016 to more than 2 million three years later.

faqs.question: What is pan de muerto and when is it eaten?
faqs.answer: Pan de muerto is a sweet bread baked for Día de Muertos and placed on the ofrenda. In 1970s Mexico City it was sold only from about 28 October to 3 November; in the Sierra de Texcoco the altar bread belongs to the dead until midday on 2 November.

faqs.question: Why are marigolds used for Day of the Dead?
faqs.answer: Cempasúchil petals are laid in a path from the street to the altar to guide the dead home, as recorded in Texcoco villages at midday on 1 November. In one Veracruz municipality, researchers found the flower is grown for the festival and nothing else.

faqs.question: What is a calavera literaria?
faqs.answer: It is a short rhyming verse in which Death comes for a living person, usually to tease them about a habit. They are written for schools, newspapers and messages around 1 and 2 November.

faqs.question: Is it disrespectful to celebrate Halloween in Mexico?
faqs.answer: Not in itself; many Mexican families do both. Be careful around people keeping an ofrenda for someone who died recently, and keep Halloween jokes away from cemeteries on 1 and 2 November.

faqs.question: What day of the week is Halloween in Mexico in 2026 and 2027?
faqs.answer: Halloween is Saturday 31 October 2026 and Sunday 31 October 2027. Día de Muertos follows on Sunday 1 and Monday 2 November 2026, and Monday 1 and Tuesday 2 November 2027.

# Halloween in Mexico and Día de Muertos: How the Two Nights Meet

Halloween in Mexico is a costume-and-sweets night on 31 October that runs straight into Día de Muertos (Day of the Dead), the family remembrance of 1 and 2 November. In 2026 that stretch is Saturday to Monday; in 2027 it is Sunday to Tuesday, and none of the three days is a statutory rest day under Mexico's federal labour law.

For anyone greeting a friend in Mexico over those nights: across SubhSandesh, 48.3% of shared pages get opened on a phone and 38.5% of creators lock theirs with a password; both are platform-wide figures, since we hold no Halloween-specific numbers. Below: a dated calendar from fieldwork, six customs, the Americanisation debate and original calaveras.

## What is the difference between Halloween and Día de Muertos?

Halloween is a night of costumes, parties and children asking for sweets, which reached Mexico from the United States largely through television. Día de Muertos is a household rite of the Catholic feasts of Todos los Santos (All Saints, 1 November) and Fieles Difuntos (All Souls, 2 November), in which families set an ofrenda (offering altar) and expect their dead to visit.

The two blurred early. Design scholar Carlos Mercado Limones recalls a Mexico City childhood about 45 years before [his October 2016 essay for UAM's *Espacio Diseño*](https://espaciodisenoojs.xoc.uam.mx/index.php/espaciodiseno/article/download/1679/1676), when television had already taught children to "reinterpret Halloween" on the night of 1 November. They cut faces into shoeboxes and went door to door asking for their calaverita, then counted coins over hot chocolate and pan de muerto.

## The dead-days calendar, 27 October to 2 November

The shorthand on most pages is "children on 1 November, adults on 2 November". Fieldwork is less tidy. In [a 2020 study in UNAM's *Estudios de Cultura Náhuatl*](https://nahuatl.historicas.unam.mx/index.php/ecn/article/view/78017), INAH anthropologist David Lorente Fernández recorded the Nahua villages of the Sierra de Texcoco, east of Mexico City.

In Santa Catarina del Monte the "accidentados" (accident victims) arrive on 28 October, the "limbitos" (unbaptised infants) on 29 October, baptised children on 30 October and adults on 31 October and 1 November; all leave on 2 November. In nearby San Jerónimo Amanalco, children arrive at midday on 31 October and leave on 1 November, when the adults come. The table sets that record against Halloween, with weekdays for 2026 and 2027.

| Date | 2026 | 2027 | Texcoco record (Lorente Fernández 2020) | Where Halloween sits |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 27–30 October | Tue–Fri | Wed–Sat | Bread baked from about 27 Oct; accident victims, infants, then children arrive 28–30 Oct | Pan de muerto in bakeries, from about 28 Oct in 1970s Mexico City |
| 31 October | Saturday | Sunday | Adults arrive (Santa Catarina); children arrive at midday (Amanalco) | Halloween night: costumes, parties, calaverita |
| 1 November | Sunday | Monday | Midday: a path of cempasúchil petals laid from the street to the altar | Todos los Santos; the calaverita night of 1970s Mexico City |
| 2 November | Monday | Tuesday | Midday church bells mark the souls' departure; families take bread and fruit to the graves | Fieles Difuntos; Halloween is over |

The takeaway: Halloween night lands inside the Day of the Dead, not before it. In some villages the dead are already home when children knock on 31 October.

## Six customs you will see between 31 October and 2 November

### 1. Pedir calaverita (asking for the little skull)

**Term:** *calaverita*, "little skull", the treat or coins a child asks for. **When:** the nights of 31 October to 2 November. **Where:** city neighbourhoods and towns alike. **Fact:** Mercado Limones writes that around 1970 almost nobody gave sweets; children collected coins in improvised shoebox money boxes, and nobody bothered with costumes.

### 2. Ofrenda (the offering altar)

**Term:** *ofrenda*, "offering". **When:** set up in the days before 1 November and lifted after 2 November. **Where:** homes, schools, offices and plazas. **Fact:** Lorente Fernández records that families clean the house first, because the dead are received "like important people", with fruit, stews, candles and bread laid out on tiered altars.

### 3. Cempasúchil (Mexican marigold)

**Term:** *cempasúchil*, the Nahuatl-derived name for *Tagetes erecta*. **When:** in greatest demand in October and November. **Where:** markets, roadside stalls and altars. **Fact:** in a [2020 *Agro Productividad* supply-chain study](https://www.revista-agroproductividad.org/index.php/agroproductividad/article/view/1847) of Tempoal, Veracruz, 83% of people surveyed said they would pay MXN 15–20 a bunch, and the authors found the flower had no local use outside Xantolo, the Huasteca name for the festival.

### 4. Pan de muerto (bread of the dead)

**Term:** *pan de muerto*, a sweet bread often topped with dough "bones". **When:** in the 1970s Mexico City bakeries stocked it from about 28 October and stopped by 3 November, per Mercado Limones. **Where:** bakeries, which in 1970s Mexico City painted Posada-style skulls on their windows in mid-October. **Fact:** in the Sierra de Texcoco the dead "own" the altar bread until the church bells ring at midday on 2 November.

### 5. Calaveras literarias (literary skulls)

**Term:** *calaveras*, short rhyming verses in which Death comes for someone still alive. **When:** written for schools, newspapers and group chats around 1 and 2 November. **Where:** in print, online and read aloud. **Fact:** Mercado Limones dates the Catrina's current fame to the 1988 opening of Mexico City's Museo Mural Diego Rivera, which revived Rivera's Catrina and José Guadalupe Posada's Calavera Garbancera.

### 6. The Mexico City parade

**Term:** *Gran Desfile de Día de Muertos*. **When:** around the Day of the Dead; the city announces the exact date each year. **Where:** central Mexico City. **Fact:** media scholar Viola Rühse shows in [*InMedia* (2021 issue, online January 2022)](https://journals.openedition.org/inmedia/2985) that the real parade began in 2016, a year after the James Bond film *Spectre* filmed a fictional one with 1,600 extras. About 1,000 performers took part in 2016, spectators rose from 425,000 that year to more than 2,000,000 three years later, and it did not run in 2020.

## Does Mexico celebrate Halloween, or resist it?

Both. Mercado Limones says that in the 1980s Halloween "seemed to be winning the battle of identity": discos hosted costume nights of Draculas and mummies, and children carried plastic pumpkins "made in China" while home altars faded.

Rühse adds two counterweights. A children's parade in Oaxaca in the 1990s was inspired by American Halloween, and Mexico's tourism ministry has promoted Día de Muertos since 1971. Yet recent years also show a political effort to set the Mexican celebration apart from the US Halloween, which honours no dead.

The parade sits in the middle of that argument. Rühse calls *Spectre*'s fictional procession "Halloween-influenced" and quotes anthropologist Claudio Lomnitz, who saw the real one as an image of Mexican culture "composed with the views of foreigners in mind".

## Is Halloween or Día de Muertos a day off in Mexico?

No. Article 74 of the [Ley Federal del Trabajo](https://www.diputados.gob.mx/LeyesBiblio/pdf/LFT.pdf) (Federal Labour Law, last reformed 14 May 2026) lists the mandatory rest days: 1 January, the first Monday of February, the third Monday of March, 1 May, 16 September, the third Monday of November, 25 December, the presidential handover every six years, and election days.

Neither 31 October, 1 November nor 2 November is on that list. In 2026, 2 November is a Monday and a normal working day under federal law, while the Revolution Day holiday falls on Monday 16 November. In 2027 those are Tuesday 2 November and Monday 15 November.

## Original calaveras and greeting lines in Spanish

These calaveras, written for this page, follow the old pattern in which Death comes for someone and fails. Three shorter lines for 31 October or 2 November follow them.

- "La Flaca llegó a tu puerta / con su vestido de gala, / pero al ver tu cocina abierta / se quedó a comer en la sala." *(Skinny Death came to your door in her party dress, but seeing your kitchen open, she stayed to eat in the living room.)*
- "Mi amiga la puntual / nunca llega a ningún lado; / la Muerte, por ser formal, / la esperó y se ha jubilado." *(My friend "the punctual one" never gets anywhere on time; Death, being polite, waited for her and has since retired.)*
- "La Muerte vino por ti / con su catrín y su flor, / mas se fue diciendo: 'Aquí / no cabe nadie, hay mucho amor.'" *(Death came for you with her dandy and her flower, but left saying: "No one else fits here, there is too much love.")*

- "Hoy pido calaverita, mañana pongo flores." *(Tonight I ask for my little skull, tomorrow I lay the flowers.)*
- "Que el cempasúchil te marque el camino a casa." *(May the marigold mark your way home.)*
- "Feliz Halloween hoy, y que tu ofrenda brille el día dos." *(Happy Halloween today, and may your altar glow on the second.)*

## Sending a Halloween greeting to one person in Mexico

A calavera in a chat lands fast, yet a playful Halloween greeting fits the friend or partner who loves the 31 October side of the week. Our [Halloween card where they knock on a haunted house and carve a jack-o'-lantern](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) is roughly a five-minute build with six photos at most, and its kids mode keeps everything spooky-cute. If you want your voice in it, the [premium Halloween page with a voice note and unlock time](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) is roughly a ten-minute build, carries 12 photos and a voice clip of up to 60 seconds, and can stay sealed until the evening of 31 October.

A shared SubhSandesh page averages 11.1 views, so expect rereads. If your partner is simply far away this season, an [I miss you page for a partner abroad](https://subhsandesh.in/missyou-gf) says so more directly.

## When to skip the Halloween page in Mexico

If your friend is building an ofrenda for someone who died this year, skip the "Will you be my boo?" card. Día de Muertos is remembrance, and a bouncing pumpkin reads as careless next to a new photograph on the altar; a phone call or a short line in Spanish does more.

Each template's menus are in English only, which may lose a grandmother who reads only Spanish. Each is built for one recipient, so it will not run a school ofrenda contest or a street party, and with 48.3% of views on a phone, keep the letter short.

## Sources

- Mercado Limones, *Espacio Diseño* 244, UAM, October 2016.
- Lorente Fernández, *Estudios de Cultura Náhuatl* 60, UNAM, 2020.
- Barajas-Rodríguez et al., *Agro Productividad* 13(3), 2020.
- Rühse, *InMedia* 9.1, online 15 January 2022.
- *Ley Federal del Trabajo*, Article 74, Cámara de Diputados, last reformed 14 May 2026.

structuralLimitations: No Halloween usage data exists in facts.md; the three first-party figures are platform-wide and labelled as such in the body.

gob.mx (Secretaría de Cultura, Agricultura, SIAP, INPI) returns a 'Challenge Validation' bot wall to scripted fetches; per BRIEF §9 it was not worked around, so no gob.mx page is cited. The LFT comes from diputados.gob.mx instead. HAL (shs.hal.science) Posada paper also returned a bot page and was dropped. search.scielo.org returned 403.
The 2026 Mexico City parade date could not be verified (the CDMX/gob.mx announcement pages sit behind the same wall), so the post gives no date for it.

Calaveras literarias: no fetchable scholarly source on the verse form itself was read; the definition is stated as general knowledge and the only sourced claim (Catrina/Posada iconography after 1988) comes from Mercado Limones.

The 'children on 1 Nov, adults on 2 Nov' shorthand in the task prompt is a generalisation; Lorente Fernández (2020) records different arrival days in two Texcoco villages (children 30 Oct or 31 Oct), so the post presents the fieldwork rather than the shorthand.
Brandes 2000 (redalyc, Alteridades) — the standard Mexico Halloween source — was deliberately not reused because b4 halloween-around-the-world built its Mexico entry on it.

Espacio Diseño is a UAM Xochimilco faculty magazine (essay, not double-blind peer reviewed); the peer-reviewed sources are Estudios de Cultura Náhuatl, InMedia and Agro Productividad. InMedia (CC BY-NC) and ECN (CC BY-NC-ND) are cited and linked only, nothing reproduced.
